ANSWER OF THE INDICATED PJM TRANSMISSION OWNERS 
 TO THE MOTION TO STAY PROCEEDINGS  
 
Pursuant to Rules 212 and 2131 of the Rules of Practice and Procedure of the Federal 
Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC” or “Commission”), the Indicated PJM Transmission 
Owners (hereinafter, “Indicated TOs”)2 submit this Answer to the April 22, 2025 Joint Comments 
and Motion to Stay Proceedings and Request to Establish Settlement Judge Procedures (“Stay

2 
 
Motion”) of the Electric Power Supply Association, the PJM Power Providers Group, Calpine 
Corporation, Cogentrix Energy Power Management, LLC, Constellation Energy Generation, LLC, 
and LS Power Development, LLC (“Joint Movants”). 
I. ARGUMENT 
 
The Stay Motion is unnecessary as the record in this proceeding is clear on two 
fundamental points.  First, all parties have expressed interest in the Commission providing 
regulatory guidance as soon as possible to bring clarity and assist with the current challenges and 
disputes.  Second, the existing PJM Open Access Transmission Tariff (“PJM Tariff”) is just and 
reasonable in regard to co-location arrangements and therefore the Commission has everything it 
needs to provide the expeditious regulatory guidance everyone seeks.   
In order to take any action imposing changes to the PJM Tariff in a Federal Power Act 
(“FPA”) section 206 proceeding,3 the Commission must first find that the existing PJM Tariff is 
not just and reasonable.  No such showing has been made and thus there is no basis to pause the 
Commission’s effort to expeditiously provide guidance without first satisfying that threshold 
requirement.  Indeed, the record in this proceeding demonstrates that the existing PJM Tariff 
remains just and reasonable.  Unless and until the Commission finds to the contrary under FPA 
section 206, there are no grounds to amend the PJM Tariff.      
Numerous commenters in this proceeding address the national security implications of 
service to these new large loads.  The truth is that the national interest will be best served by a 
quick dismissal of this proceeding, and a ruling that the existing PJM Tariff remains just and 
 
 
3  16 U.S.C. § 824e.

3 
 
reasonable.  Rather than fighting about a wish list of new rules, the parties will then instead begin 
to focus on obtaining service under the rules in place today.   
a. The PJM Tariff Has Not Been Shown to Be Unjust and Unreasonable. 
In a proceeding under section 206 of the FPA, the Commission can only remedy a “rate 
[or] charge” or “any rule, regulation, practice, or contract affecting such rate [or] charge” after it 
is found to be “unjust [or] unreasonable.”4  “The burden of proving an unjust or unreasonable rate 
rests with the party that initiated the proceeding—the Commission [(as in this case)] or the third-
party complainant.”5  Only after a successful showing that the prevailing rate is unjust and 
unreasonable may the Commission order a replacement rate.6  No such showing has been made 
here. 
The Stay Motion succinctly summarizes the arguments for why the existing rate is 
purportedly unjust and unreasonable.7  The arguments boil down to the following: while the PJM 
Tariff provides that wholesale customers serving load in the PJM Interconnection L.L.C. (“PJM”) 
region should do so with Network Integration Transmission Service, a certain class of wholesale 
customer would rather take some new and different type of service that would cost them less.   
Of course, nearly everyone who buys nearly any service would rather pay less.  But in PJM, 
the transmission owners, as in virtually every other piece of the grid regulated by the Commission, 
assess on a postage-stamp basis, without consideration of the distance between load and 
generation, the embedded costs of their respective portions of the transmission grid from network 
 
 
4  Id. § 824e(a). 
5  Pub. Citizen, Inc. v. FERC, 7 F.4th 1177, 1183 (D.C. Cir. 2021). 
6  16 U.S.C. § 824e(a). 
7  See Stay Motion at 3–4.

4 
 
customers.8  As the Commission has explained, “PJM recovers the full revenue requirements of 
existing facilities (embedded costs) through its firm transmission rates.”9  And the Commission 
has in recent years continued to reject requests that loads that claim reduced system impact merit 
some new third category of lower-cost transmission service.10  
The Joint Movants seek to move past the need for a finding that the existing rate is unjust 
and unreasonable and thus ask for procedures that investigate the second step of an FPA section 
206 proceeding (fixing a new rate) while bypassing the first step.  But the first step matters.  Unless 
and until the Commission makes a finding that the existing rate is unjust and unreasonable, any 
negotiation will be unproductive.11  Most importantly, the Commission has no authority to direct 
relief under FPA section 206 absent a finding that the existing tariff is unjust and unreasonable. 
b. Reliability Is at Stake. 
The Indicated TOs, which include investor-owned utilities, municipalities, and 
cooperatives, all believe that treating co-located load as anything other than Network Load would 
increase the risk of reliability failures and resource inadequacy in PJM.  Much of what is being 
 
 
8  See, e.g., Pennsylvania-New Jersey-Maryland Interconnection, et al., 81 FERC ¶ 61,257 (1997) (adopting PJM 
pricing proposal to allow recovery of embedded transmission revenue requirement from network customers), 
corrected by, 82 FERC ¶ 61,103 (1998), and clarified in part by, 92 FERC ¶ 61,282 (2000), and review granted in 
part, vacated in part by, 295 F.3d 1 (D.C. Cir. 2002); PJM Tariff, Section 34.1 (providing for payment by network 
customers of load ratio share of embedded cost of their zone); PJM Tariff, Attachments H-1, H-1A, H-2, H-2A, H-
3, H-3D, H-7, H-7A, H-9, H-9A, H-13, and H-13A (establishing network revenue requirements for each of the 
Exelon Utilities based on the embedded costs of their respective transmission systems). 
9  PJM Interconnection L.L.C., 139 FERC ¶ 61,243, at P 78 n.105 (2012). 
10  See, e.g., Nat’l R.R. Passenger Corp. v. PPL Elec. Utils. Corp. et al., 171 FERC ¶ 61,237, order on reh’g, 173 FERC 
¶ 61,043 (2020). 
11  If the Commission were to determine that something about the existing PJM Tariff is unjust and unreasonable, the 
Commission would no doubt provide guidance on what aspect needs reform, allowing the parties to hone the 
discussion and focus on the parts that are really at issue.  Absent such guidance and direction, any settlement talks 
would be truly gargantuan in scope—and likely set the stage for further delay followed unfortunately by failure and 
then even more delay.

5 
 
proposed involves obscuring loads from the grid operator and hoping that the grid is not impacted.  
Questions raised by the North American Electric Reliability Corporation highlight the importance 
of these concerns.12  The record is clear—no matter how connected to the PJM Transmission 
System, large loads pose both a safety and a reliability concern.  It is unrealistic to ask the Indicated 
TOs to accede to these demands in the context of settlement procedures while those questions 
remain unresolved. 
II. CONCLUSION 
The national interest will not be well served if service requests under the existing rules are 
further delayed by the outcome of this proceeding in which a number of parties attempt to rewrite 
the PJM Tariff.  Instead, the best way to promote co-located load customers is to provide certainty, 
which the Commission can accomplish quickly by simply clarifying that co-located loads should 
seek service under the well-established, just and reasonable terms of the existing PJM Tariff.   
For the reasons stated above, the Indicated TOs respectfully request that the Commission 
reject the Stay Motion.   
 
 
 
 
 
12  There are profound reliability issues associated with large data center loads that are being actively investigated right 
now.  See, e.g., Comments of the North American Electric Reliability Corporation (“NERC”) (Apr. 23, 2025); Item 
E-4 Presentation by NERC at April 17, 2025 Commission meeting.
